title: Make your first commit
intro: You have a repository with one commit. You will take a change through the three places it can live: the working tree, the staging area, and the repository.

steps.say: `git status` is the command you will run most. It compares all three places and tells you what differs.
steps.after: Nothing to commit, working tree clean. All three places agree.

steps.say: Write a notes file. Git will notice it but will not track it yet.
suggest: echo "Read chapter 2 on linear algebra" > notes.md
steps.hint: The file must be named notes.md.
steps.after: Run `git status` if you like. The file is listed under Untracked files. It exists only in your working tree.

steps.say: Staging chooses what the next snapshot will contain. Nothing is saved to history yet.
steps.after: The Files panel now marks notes.md as staged. It is in the staging area, waiting.

steps.say: A commit records everything that is staged, with a message that says why.
steps.hint: Use -m to pass the message. This terminal has no editor to open.
steps.after: A second dot appeared in the graph, and `main` moved forward to it.

steps.goal: Change a tracked file and look at the difference
steps.say: `git diff` compares your working tree to the staging area, line by line.
steps.after: Lines starting with + are additions. The change is in your working tree only.

steps.goal: Stage and commit in one move
steps.say: `-a` stages every tracked file that changed, then commits. It does not pick up brand-new files.
Each line of `git log --oneline` is one snapshot, newest first.

outro: Edit, stage, commit. Every later skill in this guide is built on that loop.

title: Branch, commit, switch back
intro: A branch is a label that points at a commit. Watch the labels in the graph as you work: they move, the commits do not.

steps.say: The star marks the branch you are on. That is where HEAD points.

steps.goal: Create a branch and switch to it
steps.say: `git switch -c` creates the branch and moves you onto it in one step.
steps.after: Look at the graph: two labels on one commit. A new branch is a new pointer. No files were copied.

steps.say: Add a line to the config and commit it here.
steps.after: `try-warmup` moved forward. `main` stayed where it was.

steps.goal: Switch back to main and read the file
steps.say: Switching branches rewrites your working tree to match that branch's snapshot.
steps.after: The warmup line is gone from your working tree. It is safe on the other branch.

steps.goal: Make a different commit on main
steps.say: Now make main move too, so the two branches diverge.
steps.after: The graph forks: two lines of work growing from the same commit.

steps.say: You are on main, so this brings `try-warmup` into main. The changes touch different files, so Git combines them without help.
steps.after: The new commit has two parents. That is what a merge commit is.

steps.say: The label has done its job. Deleting it removes the pointer, not the commits.

outro: Branches are cheap pointers. Create one for every piece of work, and delete it when the work lands.

title: Fetch, pull and a rejected push
intro: Your clone and GitHub each hold their own copy of the history. The lab shows both graphs. A teammate, Sam, has already pushed a commit you do not have.
setup: !teammate msg="Add contributing notes" file=CONTRIBUTING.md text="Open an issue first."

steps.say: `origin` is the conventional name for the repository you cloned from.
Fetch downloads new commits and moves `origin/main`. It never touches your own branch or your files.
steps.after: In your graph, `origin/main` is now one commit ahead of `main`. You have Sam's commit but have not used it.

steps.say: `main..origin/main` means: commits on origin/main that main does not have.
Pull is fetch followed by merge. Your branch has no commits of its own, so the merge is a fast-forward.
Now do some work of your own.
While you were working, Sam pushed again. Try to push and read what Git says.
before: !teammate msg="Clarify contributing notes" file=CONTRIBUTING.md text="Open an issue before large changes."
steps.after: Rejected. GitHub has a commit you lack, and Git will not overwrite someone else's work to make room for yours.

steps.say: Bring Sam's commit in, then publish. You and Sam changed different files, so the merge is automatic.
steps.after: The pull made a merge commit joining the two lines. The push then moved GitHub's main forward.

outro: Fetch looks. Pull integrates. Push publishes, and only when you already have everything the remote has.

title: A pull request from the terminal
intro: On this practice remote, main is protected, as it is on most shared repositories. Changes reach main through a pull request. You will run the whole loop with git and gh.

steps.goal: Create a branch for the work
steps.say: One branch per piece of work. Name it for what it does.
Add an evaluation script and commit it on the branch.
`-u` links your local branch to the one on GitHub, so later you can type `git push` alone.
steps.after: The GitHub graph now has your branch. main there is untouched.

steps.say: A pull request proposes merging your branch into main and gives the change a place for review.
suggest: gh pr create --title "Add eval script" --body "First evaluation script. Closes #3."

steps.say: `gh pr view` shows what a reviewer would see, including whether it can merge cleanly.
Squash combines the branch into one commit on main. `--delete-branch` removes the branch on GitHub and locally, and switches you back to main.
Your local main was fast-forwarded to match GitHub.

outro: Branch, commit, push, open, merge, delete. The same loop works for one person or a hundred.

title: Restore, amend, revert
intro: Three undos, each for a different moment: before you commit, after you commit but before you push, and after you push.

steps.say: Edit a file and stage it. Then imagine you change your mind.
`git restore --staged` takes a file out of the staging area. Your edit stays in the working tree.
`git restore` without `--staged` overwrites the file with the last staged or committed version. This is the one undo here that cannot be undone, because the edit was never committed.

steps.goal: Commit with a typo in the message
steps.say: Make a real change and commit it with a misspelled message.

steps.goal: Fix the last commit with amend
steps.say: The commit is not pushed, so replacing it affects nobody. Amend makes a new commit and drops the old one.
steps.after: The commit id changed. Amend never edits a commit in place. It writes a replacement.

steps.say: Push the commit. From this moment other people may have it.
Suppose batch size 64 was wrong. History is now shared, so do not rewrite it. Revert adds a new commit that applies the opposite change.
A revert is an ordinary commit, so an ordinary push works. Nobody has to repair their clone.

outro: Unstage before committing, amend before pushing, revert after pushing.

title: Resolve a merge conflict
intro: Your branch `tune-lr` lowered the learning rate. Meanwhile main raised it and added a warmup line. Both changed the same line of `config.yaml`. You are on `tune-lr`.
setup: git commit -am "Raise learning rate with warmup"

steps.say: Before merging, see how the two branches differ. Lines with - are main's version and lines with + are yours.
Bring main into your branch. Git will stop when it reaches the line both sides changed.
steps.after: CONFLICT is a report, not a failure. Git merged what it could and is waiting for your decision on the rest.

steps.say: `git status` lists the unmerged file. `cat` shows the markers Git wrote into it.
steps.after: Above the `=======` line is your side (HEAD). Below it is main's side. The first and last lines of the file merged cleanly.

steps.goal: Back out, to prove you can
steps.say: The exit is always open. Abort returns everything to the moment before the merge.
Same merge, same conflict. This time you will finish it.
Keep your lower learning rate and main's warmup line. Tap config.yaml in the Files panel and edit it by hand, or overwrite it with the command below. All three marker lines must go.
steps.hint: The file still contains a marker line, or no longer has an lr line.
steps.after: The right answer was neither side. It was a third version that respects both changes.

steps.say: Staging is how you tell Git a conflicted file is settled.
Git prepared the merge message for you, so a bare `git commit` is enough.
The merge commit has two parents and records your resolution.

outro: Stop, read both sides, write the text you want, stage, commit. The procedure never changes.

title: Merge commit, squash and rebase side by side
intro: One branch, three ways to land it. You will try each, rewind, and compare the shape of the history each leaves behind. Rewinding is safe here because nothing has been pushed.

steps.say: This is what **Create a merge commit** does on a pull request. Every commit on the branch is kept, joined to main by one new commit.
steps.after: The graph shows a loop: the branch leaves main and comes back.

steps.say: Move main back one commit, before the merge. The first parent of a merge commit is where main was.
This is **Squash and merge**. The whole branch becomes one staged change, which you commit as a single commit on main.
steps.after: One tidy commit on main. The branch's own commits are not in main's history, so Git does not see the branch as merged.

steps.say: Drop the squash commit.
Rebase replays the branch's commits on top of main's latest commit. They get new ids, because their parent changed.
steps.after: The branch now starts from the tip of main. The original two commits are dashed in the graph: unreachable, but still in the reflog.

steps.say: main has nothing the branch lacks, so merging only slides the label forward. This is the result of **Rebase and merge**.
The log is a straight line. The reflog remembers every place HEAD has been, including the merge commit and the squash commit you discarded.

outro: A merge commit keeps the true shape. Squash keeps main readable. Rebase keeps every commit in a straight line. Teams pick one and stay consistent.

title: Reset three ways, stash, recover
intro: Reset moves the branch pointer. The three modes differ only in what they do to the staging area and your files. You will try each, then lose a commit on purpose and get it back.

steps.goal: Soft reset: uncommit, keep it staged
steps.say: `--soft` moves the branch back one commit and leaves the staging area and your files alone.
steps.after: The change from the dropped commit is staged, ready to commit again.

steps.say: This is the classic use of a soft reset: redo the last commit.
With no flag, reset is `--mixed`. The branch moves back and the staging area is reset. Your files keep the change.
Stash saves your uncommitted changes and gives you a clean working tree, for when you must switch tasks.
`pop` reapplies the newest stash and removes it from the stash list.

steps.goal: Commit, then destroy it with a hard reset
steps.say: `--hard` moves the branch back and overwrites the staging area and your files. The commit disappears from the log.
steps.after: The file is back to v2 and the log shows two commits. The third is dashed in the graph: nothing points at it.

steps.say: The reflog records every position HEAD has held, including the commit no branch points at.
steps.after: `HEAD@{1}` is where HEAD was one move ago: the commit you just dropped.

steps.say: Reset can move a branch forward as well as back. Point it at the reflog entry.

outro: Committed work is hard to lose. Uncommitted work is easy to lose, which is why a hard reset or a restore deserves a second look.

title: Cherry-pick, amend, force with lease
intro: Your branch `feature/augment` has three pushed commits. One is a bug fix main needs today. Another has a lazy message. You will move the fix, tidy the branch, and update the remote without endangering anyone else's work.

steps.say: Read the branch's history. The middle commit is the one main needs.
Cherry-pick copies one commit's change onto the branch you are on. `feature/augment~1` means one commit before the tip.
steps.after: main has the fix and none of the unfinished augmentation work. The copy has a new id: same change, different parent.

steps.goal: Reword the last commit on the feature branch
steps.say: Back on your branch, replace the lazy message.
You rewrote a commit that GitHub already has. See what a plain push does.
steps.after: Rejected. Your branch no longer contains the commit GitHub has, so this is not a fast-forward.

steps.say: `--force-with-lease` overwrites the remote branch only if it is still where you last saw it. If a teammate pushed in the meantime, it refuses.
main moved when you cherry-picked. Replay your branch on top of it. Watch what happens to the fix commit.
steps.after: The branch now has two commits of its own, not three. The fix was already on main, so replaying it changed nothing and Git dropped it.

steps.say: A rebase rewrites every replayed commit, so the remote needs a forced update again. Use the lease.

outro: Rewrite your own unshared branches freely. The moment someone else builds on a branch, treat its history as fixed.

title: Detached HEAD and the commit nobody points at
intro: HEAD normally names a branch. It can also name a commit directly. Work done there belongs to no branch, and only a ref keeps a commit alive.

steps.say: A commit is a small text object: the id of a tree, the ids of its parents, an author, a message.
steps.after: The `parent` line is the whole link to history. Change anything in a parent and its id changes, which changes this commit's id too.

steps.goal: Check out an old commit directly
steps.say: Give checkout a commit instead of a branch name.
steps.after: HEAD now holds a commit id. In the graph, the HEAD marker sits on the commit with no branch label beside it.

steps.say: You can commit here. The new commit has a parent but no branch.
suggest: git commit -am "Try label smoothing on baseline"

steps.goal: Walk away and read the warning
steps.say: Switch back to main and read every line Git prints.
steps.after: One commit left behind. Nothing points at it, so it is unreachable. Garbage collection will eventually delete unreachable objects.

steps.say: The reflog still knows where HEAD has been.
Create a branch at the reflog entry. `HEAD@{1}` is where HEAD was before your last move.
steps.after: The commit is solid in the graph again. A forty-character pointer was the only difference between kept and lost.

outro: Refs make commits reachable. Reachable commits are kept. Everything else in Git follows from that.

title: Rescue commits after a bad reset
intro: It is late. You mean to drop one commit from `experiment` and type the wrong number. Three commits vanish, including your best result. Nothing was pushed. Recover using only what Git keeps locally.

steps.say: Run the command as you would have typed it.
Do not commit, and do not run cleanup commands. First find out what state you are in.
steps.after: The log shows one commit. The reset moved a pointer. The three commits still exist as unreachable objects, dashed in the graph.

steps.say: Every move of HEAD is recorded with the commit it pointed at.
`HEAD@{1}` is the position before the reset.
A tag is a permanent name for one commit. Tag the commit behind any number you report.
The reflog is local and its entries expire. A pushed branch is the durable backup.

outro: Recovery worked because the work was committed. Commit early, push often, and tag what you cite.

title: Free play
intro: No goals here. A small repository with a remote and a second branch, ready for experiments. Type `help` to see what the terminal supports. Reset the lab whenever you want a clean start.
outro: Break things. That is what a sandbox is for.
